title: The missing letter (Berakhot 4b)
hookLine: Psalm 145 runs through the alphabet but skips nun, the teachers say to avoid a verse about falling
carry: the Lord upholdeth all that fall
last: THANKS IS THE PART MEANT TO LAST.

cards: Psalm one hundred forty-five is an acrostic. Each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet: alef, bet, gimel, and on down the line.

The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, makes a large promise about it: whoever says it three times a day is assured a place in the world to come. It sits at the heart of the prayer called Ashrei. But count the verses.
The Hebrew alphabet has twenty-two letters. This psalm has twenty-one verses. One letter, partway through, is missing.

teach.b: The missing letter is nun, the letter for the sound N. The Talmud asks why. Rabbi Yochanan answers: because a terrible verse begins with nun.

teach.h: FALLEN, SHE SHALL RISE NO MORE.
teach.b: In the prophet Amos: fallen is the maiden Israel, she shall rise no more. Nafelah, fallen, starts with nun. So, the teachers say, the psalmist left the letter out rather than bring that word near a song of praise.
Then another rabbi, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, adds the beautiful part. Even so, he says, David came back and caught them.
Look at the very next verse, the one beginning with samech, the letter after nun. In the old Jewish translation: "The LORD upholdeth all that fall, and raiseth up all those that are bowed down."
The word fall is right there, not as a sentence, but as something caught. The fall is acknowledged, then held. Now, what does the scholar hear?

teach.h: A NUN LINE IN THE DEAD SEA SCROLLS.
teach.b: Among the Dead Sea Scrolls is a copy of this psalm that does have a nun verse: God is faithful in his words, and gracious in all his deeds.
The ancient Greek translation has one too. So some scholars think a nun line once existed and dropped out of the traditional Hebrew text. The Talmud's reading doesn't depend on that question.
It's a teaching about how to sing: you can leave a painful word unsaid, and still, in the next breath, say that the fallen are lifted.

how: Ashrei, built around Psalm 145, is said twice in the morning service and once in the afternoon service; in the morning it is the center of the verses of song.

games.q: you're writing an alphabet song of praise. the letter nun brings to mind a verse about Israel falling and never rising. what do you do?
o: use the verse anyway; it's honest.
leave the letter out, and catch the fallen in the next verse.
games.why: that's the Talmud's reading: nun is left out, and the next verse says the LORD upholdeth all that fall.

practice: Think back over the last few weeks for a moment when someone could have said the hard thing and didn't: a friend who let your mistake go, a parent who let a bad grade go, someone who changed the subject to spare you.
Picture the word they didn't say, then what they did instead: a hand on your shoulder, a joke, a lift home. That's the samech after the missing nun.

wordCard.voice: Nun. The letter for the sound N, left out of Psalm one hundred forty-five, the Talmud says, so the song never speaks of falling without catching.
